en: BÉATRICE : No.
EUSTACHE : What?
BÉATRICE : You are not happy. Besides, it isn't true, it makes no sense... What is happening is too horrible to hurt right away, that is all. But don't be afraid, it will come.
EUSTACHE : I can easily put myself in your place, and I admit...
BÉATRICE : No, please...
EUSTACHE : It's completely sincere.

BÉATRICE : The only resource left to me is to try to understand... (She looks at him.) You no longer have your expression of these past months, that's certain... So that was what you needed: a hard, vicious woman to take you, to love you brutally after terrifying you... (Her face convulses.) It's hideous...
EUSTACHE : Béatrice!

BÉATRICE : A woman without the slightest tenderness, but who... (Abruptly.) I don't understand anything. That kind of barb, that poisoned sting—surely that trollop didn't tear it out of you? Tell me... I don't understand anything.
EUSTACHE : Listen to me, Béatrice... When I went to her place the other day, I swear to you...
BÉATRICE : But I know that very well.
EUSTACHE : What tormented me was only anxiety, pity... fear.
BÉATRICE : Not only that... not only that. Shame, too. Your sickness, your only sickness.
EUSTACHE : She sensed my anguish... she began to weep.
BÉATRICE : She must have been beautiful...
EUSTACHE : I had never seen her weep. And then...
BÉATRICE : Yes, yes, don't bother; what followed doesn't interest me in the least.
EUSTACHE : And something physical arose between us, obviously, physical. A need, an attraction.

BÉATRICE : If you brought that woman here in my absence, it was because you wanted to destroy our union, to wreck it, so that nothing of it remained, so that everything would be finished, soiled, annihilated. Wasn't it?
EUSTACHE : Remember the letter I wrote to the ministry.
BÉATRICE : Do you really think it's of the same order?
EUSTACHE : Yes. There must be something decisive in my life.
BÉATRICE : Something decisive... A decision is another matter.
EUSTACHE : I can't let myself drift any longer.
BÉATRICE : My poor Eustache!... So... we divorce... and you live together?
EUSTACHE : She counts on it.
BÉATRICE : What?
EUSTACHE : I say that she counts on it...
BÉATRICE : And you?
EUSTACHE : I don't think I can disappoint her.
BÉATRICE : There is an answer that might not give her much pleasure.
EUSTACHE : I am the one who doesn't understand. You accept?
BÉATRICE : As much as you do. Neither more nor less.
EUSTACHE : You are smiling?
BÉATRICE : That doesn't prevent my heart from heaving with disgust. It is as though someone had stirred up all the foul mire at the bottom of life. What a stench! But you smell it too.

EUSTACHE, pointing toward the bedroom: I have lived too long in this house. This interior exasperates me; too much floor polish everywhere, too many flowers in the vases, too many graceful details. I long for the sordid like a deliverance.
BÉATRICE, with a cry: Eustache, the sordidness... but it is in you! (A silence.)
EUSTACHE : What do you expect me to become? There is no war, no epidemic, no occasion to die. Suicide—perhaps I am not brave enough, or not cowardly enough, whichever you like.

BÉATRICE : Listen to me: I will not let you leave. We will go together, wherever you want, to another country, beyond the seas if you wish. You can easily obtain a leave of absence. A change of scene, you understand, a clean break. That is what is needed. Nothing else... And what happened... I promise to think of it only as a bout of fever, of delirium...
EUSTACHE, faintly: No...

BÉATRICE : When I think of all that has happened since the other day... of Werner, of Gisela... (Eustache stirs.) It seems to me as though a wind of disease has blown over our house. (In an altered voice.) I myself am not sure that I completely resisted. That is precisely why we must leave... to rid ourselves of these miasmas. Otherwise we shall not succeed. If you wish... It's an idea that has just come to me for the first time... we will go to Russia.
EUSTACHE : I don't want to go there as a tourist. It disgusts me.
BÉATRICE : Naturally. But one must be able to live somewhere other than a hotel, to make contact with life... We would learn Russian...
EUSTACHE : That isn't easy. It would have been better to think of it sooner.
BÉATRICE : You didn't have time.
EUSTACHE : I have to think. I no longer know where I stand, I can't see clearly anymore.
BÉATRICE : I am here.
[SCENE VII]
THE SAME, WERNER.
BÉATRICE : Werner!
WERNER : Forgive me, perhaps I come a little late.
BÉATRICE : Not at all.
EUSTACHE : You are welcome.
WERNER : In any case, I have come to say goodbye. I leave tomorrow.
EUSTACHE : You are leaving Paris?
WERNER : And even France.
EUSTACHE : Where are you going? To Switzerland?
WERNER : No.
BÉATRICE : You have lost weight, Werner... Is there any news?
WERNER : You mean about my wife? It will be better if we do not speak of Gisela. She has left with Baron Schratz von Hummelstein, I know it now. They must be in Rio de Janeiro by now.
BÉATRICE : It is inconceivable. She thought only of returning to Germany.
WERNER : She will return there under the best possible conditions, rest assured. But I shall be there before her. That, she had not foreseen.
EUSTACHE : You are going back to Germany?
WERNER : Yes.
EUSTACHE : What happened? Did you see Wetzinger again?
WERNER : No. There is no impresario for this kind of return.
EUSTACHE : Come, explain yourself.
WERNER : I am not sure that I can give you many explanations.

EUSTACHE : In short, the Nazis have nothing specific to reproach you with. You will easily be able to rebuild your career over there. Especially since, because of the expulsions, the competition must have decreased noticeably.

WERNER, with restrained force: Eustache, I think you had better leave me alone with Béatrice, otherwise we might end up exchanging rather harsh words, and perhaps not only words. That would be a pity, for it is almost certain we will never see each other again.
EUSTACHE : Perfect. It even works out all the better, as I am having dinner with Gertrude in Montparnasse. (He goes out.)
[SCENE VIII]
WERNER : Forgive me... I'll wait another moment... I want to be completely calm. It is not very easy.
BÉATRICE : I still cannot bear the thought that it was here your marriage was shattered.

WERNER, with deep sorrow: Gisela needed only a pretext to leave me; she would have found one no matter what. Even before leaving Germany, we had quarrels, not only over Rudolf. She had already had a lover, a composer. He was married; she believed he would divorce his wife to marry her. But I knew he wouldn't. Ever since that episode, I never believed it would be long before the separation. When misfortune struck, I thought: perhaps all the same... but the opposite happened. Gisela is not a woman who can live in misfortune.
BÉATRICE : You have forgiven her...

WERNER : I do not know exactly. It depends on the day, on memories, on my mood... When I am with you I think I have; but that is perhaps... that proves nothing. One must wait for the end. I suppose it is only when there is nothing left to hope for, when everything is already decided... There is something else I wanted to tell you that may perhaps surprise you. I don't yet understand it completely myself... Sometimes I think that there was a sickness here, and that I caught it in another form. A kind of infectious flu.
BÉATRICE : You too...

WERNER : I am living in a very quiet boardinghouse near the Observatory. That is to say, it isn't really a boardinghouse. It is two ladies living in an apartment far too large; they have two floors, and all kinds of people live there. French students, and also English, Norwegians. Very kind people. They took to me right away. It's very strange. I have already been invited to three or four families for the coming holidays.
BÉATRICE : That is very good!
WERNER : Ah, it is not good at all. (A silence.)
BÉATRICE : Why, Werner?
WERNER : Mme Brossard said to me: what luck! you are not a communist! Miss Johnson said to me: what luck! you are not a Jew! and things like that...
BÉATRICE : And so?

WERNER : Jacques Richemond congratulated me because I was a German from another age, and Mlle Timonnier because I didn't wear glasses... Besides, I wear them now when I read... And the other day I sang a Schubert song: it was unbearable.
BÉATRICE : Why?
WERNER : An idiotic enthusiasm.
BÉATRICE : I don't understand at all... There are irritating people everywhere; this isn't the first time you have encountered them, I suppose... or is it?...
WERNER : Go on.
BÉATRICE : No, I am asking you to explain.
WERNER : It is very simple. Soon I will have no money left. I had the sum I had in Switzerland transferred to Gisela. I didn't know yet about Baron Schratz. But I don't regret it...
BÉATRICE : And yet, Werner, if you are short of funds, you know very well that your friends...
WERNER : Eustache is no longer my friend. Besides, he has done enough.
BÉATRICE : But I...

WERNER : That is completely impossible. Besides, you are mistaken. I am not afraid of starving. I tell you that I am already invited here, there, and elsewhere. And in all those places I know in advance that I will meet other people.
BÉATRICE : That is very beautiful.
WERNER : You don't seriously think so.
BÉATRICE : But I do, Werner... it is because you are the man you are that this chain of friendships forms around you...
WERNER : A chain... perhaps I have no desire to let myself be chained.
BÉATRICE : You are playing on words.
WERNER : No, Béatrice; if there is in me, as you say, something that wins hearts, I cannot profit from it, I cannot live on it, I cannot get ahead through sympathy.
BÉATRICE : It seems to me that you are yielding to a completely excessive scruple.

WERNER : Perhaps it is a scruple; I would say more: perhaps Eustache passed it on to me in some way... like the flu. That is possible. But at other moments I wonder whether this thought does not come from much further away, from much higher up... (More softly.) Rudolf was ugly, he always wore glasses; his ears stuck out. He did not appeal to young girls or young women. There was no danger of him getting ahead through sympathy. He would have starved to death, perhaps.
BÉATRICE : You told me that in America...
WERNER : A committee was formed after his death. Only after his death. Over there they are going to publish piano pieces that are actually worth next to nothing. It is only because he is dead...
BÉATRICE, with anguish: But then, what are you going to do?

WERNER : I told you that I am returning to Germany. I will be arrested. I expect to be arrested. I have done what was necessary for that. These past evenings I have been in cafés with German communists. The Nazis are very well informed, you know. I am sufficiently compromised.
BÉATRICE : And then?
WERNER : It is probable they will send me to a concentration camp.
BÉATRICE : That is horrible.
WERNER : That is why I am returning to Germany.
BÉATRICE, in a trembling voice: I don't quite understand, I assure you.
WERNER : There is not so much to understand. Sympathy, at Mme Brossard's, is irritating, it is idiotic; in a concentration camp, perhaps it is a source of strength.
BÉATRICE, passionately: But, Werner, if they shoot you?
WERNER, simply: It is not impossible, but I don't think so at all.
BÉATRICE : This return is suicide.
WERNER : Absolutely not, Béatrice, you are mistaken. Suicide is a crime.
BÉATRICE, in a toneless voice: I don't see the difference.
WERNER : An enormous difference. I am simply placing myself at disposal.
BÉATRICE : Of whom, Werner? Of what? Of the cause? Of the revolution?
WERNER : The cause does not interest me; human beings interest me, though Eustache believed the opposite.
BÉATRICE, bitterly: Do not speak of Eustache.
WERNER : I am now completely calm.
BÉATRICE : I am the one who is calm no longer. What is going to happen to you is his fault too.
WERNER : No, Béatrice, I do not believe so. Quite the contrary, in fact...

BÉATRICE : What do you mean? (The telephone rings. Béatrice picks up the receiver.) Hello!... Is that you, Mother? It is Béatrice speaking... No, not Eustache, Béatrice... yes, Béatrice. Eustache has gone out... I don't know, late in the evening, I suppose... I can hardly hear you; you must not be speaking quite into the receiver... Yes, I know you don't like the telephone... What is the matter?... But no, come now, you must not take it tragically... Léontine told you?... An old people's home?... What madness! Never, come now, never would Eustache... nor Adrien... When people are angry, they say many things... She was in the wrong, besides, entirely in the wrong... I don't dream of excusing her... Ah? I didn't know... In four months... Come have lunch with me tomorrow... Eustache? Why yes, I suppose so... Do come. Everything will work out, you'll see... Sending you my love... (She hangs up.) My sister-in-law is expecting a baby. (A silence.)

WERNER : There is another thing I have seen since leaving Sèvres. I did not know until the last moment whether I would tell you. But I must, so that you will not be unjust... toward Eustache. I believe he understood very quickly what we ourselves doubtless refused to understand... it was in our interest to close our eyes. He too, perhaps, but he could not. And at the same time he could make no reproach against us; we never gave him cause to. Perhaps that was not fair. He is one of those men who need others to be in the wrong toward them.
BÉATRICE : Werner, you cannot mean that we...
WERNER : Exactly that. And we knew it from the very first day. (Béatrice bows her head.) And it is also for that reason that I am returning to Germany.
BÉATRICE, convulsively: You must not...

WERNER : Everything could now become clouded, like spring water after the rain... But only for a few minutes... Since I shall be elsewhere and will not even be able to write to you anymore. Then everything will become pure again...
BÉATRICE : You will not write to me?
WERNER : It would be impossible, and besides, Eustache could not bear it.
BÉATRICE : He wants to leave with that woman.
WERNER : He will not leave. Everything depends on you, Béatrice; you know it well.
BÉATRICE : Will I have the strength to hold him back? Do I even have the desire?

WERNER, forcefully: You cannot abandon him. You must always remember that you are the wife of a poor man... Poverty is not the lack of money, or the lack of success. Eustache had money, he had success: he remained poor, ever poorer; he will probably never be cured of his poverty. It is the greatest evil of our time, spreading like a plague; no physician has yet been found to treat it. People do not even know how to recognize it. The artist will escape it, no doubt, even if he does not have enough to eat. And also the believer who has prayer... All the others are threatened.
BÉATRICE : You are asking me to live beside a leper...

WERNER : Leper colonies are going to multiply across the earth, I fear. It will be a grace reserved for very few to live there knowing that one lives among lepers, and without shrinking from them in horror. Even more than a grace. How do you say it? viaticum... a viaticum.
BÉATRICE : I am not brave enough, Werner, I assure you.

WERNER : You will think of me as I think of Rudolf. Later I shall inhabit you as Rudolf inhabits me... And you will recall then what I said to you some weeks ago: if there were only the living, Béatrice...
